title: Portfolio Managers
blurb: For PMS fund managers: portfolio construction, equity and bond strategies, risk, performance measurement and the SEBI rules you operate under.

units.title: Investment landscape and securities markets
units.overview: Investing versus speculation, objectives and constraints, and how primary and secondary markets work.
facts: Investing versus speculation
Investing commits capital for an expected return after analysis of value, while speculation takes a short-term bet mainly on price movement.
A manager buys a company after valuing its cash flows.
Speculation and investing differ only in the amount of money.
Return objective
A return objective states the return a portfolio needs, taking in the client's goals, inflation and the risk the client can accept.
A client needs 12% a year to fund a goal.
The return objective is fixed without reference to the client.
Risk tolerance and ability
Risk tolerance is the client's willingness to take risk, while ability is the financial capacity to bear loss; the lower of the two governs.
A willing client with little spare capital gets a cautious portfolio.
Willingness alone decides how much risk to take.
Investment constraints
Constraints such as liquidity, time horizon, tax, legal limits and unique needs restrict how a portfolio can be built.
A client who needs cash in two years cannot hold illiquid assets.
Constraints do not affect asset selection.
Primary market
In the primary market, securities are issued for the first time and the issuer receives the proceeds.
A company raises capital through an IPO.
Companies receive the money when shares trade between investors.
Secondary market
In the secondary market, existing securities are traded between investors, giving liquidity and price discovery.
A fund sells shares on the exchange.
The issuer receives funds in every secondary trade.
Clearing and settlement
A clearing corporation guarantees settlement of trades and manages counterparty risk, with delivery of securities and funds through depositories and banks.
A trade is settled through the clearing corporation.
Settlement risk is borne wholly by the buyer.
Market intermediaries
Brokers, depositories, custodians, registrars and portfolio managers each perform a distinct role in the securities chain.
A custodian safeguards client securities of a portfolio manager.
A portfolio manager also acts as the depository.

units.title: Stocks and equity research
units.overview: Equity as an asset, fundamental and technical analysis, valuation ratios and governance.
facts: Equity ownership
An equity share represents ownership in a company, with a residual claim on earnings and assets after creditors are paid.
A shareholder is paid after lenders if a firm winds up.
Shareholders rank ahead of lenders.
Top-down analysis
Top-down analysis begins with the economy, moves to industries and then selects companies.
A manager studies growth, then sectors, then stocks.
Top-down analysis starts with picking a single stock.
Bottom-up analysis
Bottom-up analysis starts with company-level research on business, management and financials, with less weight on the macro view.
An analyst picks a firm on the strength of its balance sheet.
Bottom-up analysis ignores company financials.
Price-earnings ratio
The P/E ratio is the market price divided by earnings per share and shows what investors pay per rupee of earnings.
A share at ₹200 with EPS of ₹10 has a P/E of 20.
P/E is price divided by book value.
Price-to-book ratio
P/B compares market price to book value per share and is often used for banks and asset-heavy firms.
A bank trades at 2.5 times book value.
P/B compares price to dividends.
Return on equity
ROE is net profit divided by shareholders' equity and shows how well a firm earns on owners' capital.
A firm earns ₹15 on every ₹100 of equity.
ROE measures return on total assets.
Free cash flow
Free cash flow is operating cash flow less capital expenditure, and is the cash available to capital providers.
A firm generates cash after funding its capex.
Free cash flow equals reported net profit.
Discounted cash flow
DCF values a business as the present value of its expected future cash flows, discounted at a rate reflecting risk.
An analyst discounts forecast cash flows at 12%.
DCF values a firm using past profits alone.
Technical analysis
Technical analysis studies price and volume patterns to time trades and assumes patterns tend to repeat.
A trader uses moving averages to find a trend.
Technical analysis relies on the audited balance sheet.
Corporate governance
Good governance means a transparent, accountable board that protects minority shareholders, and weak governance is an investment risk.
A manager avoids a firm with frequent related-party dealings.
Governance has no effect on valuation.
Stewardship
Institutional investors, including portfolio managers, are expected to monitor investee companies and vote in the interest of clients.
A manager votes on a resolution after reviewing it.
Voting rights on client holdings can be ignored.

units.title: Fixed income securities
units.overview: Bond features, yield, credit and interest rate risk, and valuation.
facts: Coupon and face value
A bond's coupon is the interest paid on its face value, and the face value is repaid at maturity.
A 8% bond of ₹1,000 face pays ₹80 a year.
The coupon is a share of the bond's market price.
Price and yield
Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions, so a rise in market yields lowers the price.
Rates rise and an existing bond loses value.
Bond prices rise when market yields rise.
Yield to maturity
YTM is the single discount rate that equates the bond's price to the present value of its cash flows if held to maturity.
A bond bought below par has a YTM above its coupon.
YTM is always equal to the coupon rate.
Current yield
Current yield is annual coupon divided by the current market price.
A ₹80 coupon on a bond priced at ₹950 gives a current yield above 8%.
Current yield includes the capital gain at maturity.
Duration
Duration measures the sensitivity of a bond's price to interest rate changes, and a longer duration means more rate risk.
A long bond falls more than a short bond when yields rise.
Duration measures credit risk.
Credit risk
Credit risk is the risk that the issuer fails to pay interest or principal, which credit ratings help assess.
An investor requires a higher yield on a lower-rated bond.
Credit risk is the same for all bonds of a firm's group.
Reinvestment risk
Reinvestment risk is the chance that coupons are reinvested at lower rates than the original yield.
Falling rates reduce income from reinvested coupons.
Reinvestment risk applies only to zero-coupon bonds.
Zero-coupon bond
A zero-coupon bond pays no periodic interest and is issued at a discount to face value, repaying face value at maturity.
A bond bought at ₹700 repays ₹1,000.
A zero-coupon bond pays a high monthly coupon.
Yield curve
The yield curve plots yields against maturity, and an upward-sloping curve means longer maturities have higher yields.
Ten-year yields are above one-year yields.
A normal yield curve slopes downward.
Government securities
Government securities carry sovereign backing and little credit risk, and set the benchmark for other yields.
Corporate bond spreads are measured over a G-sec yield.
G-secs carry high default risk.

units.title: Derivatives and mutual funds
units.overview: Futures and options, how portfolio managers use them, and mutual funds as a comparison and a building block.
facts: Derivative
A derivative is a contract whose value is derived from an underlying asset, index or rate.
A futures contract on an index.
A derivative has its own value independent of any underlying.
Futures contract
A futures contract is a standardised agreement to buy or sell an asset at a set price on a future date, with daily settlement.
A manager sells index futures to cover a falling market.
A futures contract gives only the right, not the obligation, to trade.
Option
An option gives the buyer the right but not the obligation to buy or sell at a strike price, for a premium paid to the seller.
A put option protects a holding against a fall.
The option buyer must always exercise.
Hedging
Hedging uses derivatives to reduce an existing risk, such as selling futures against a stock portfolio.
A manager hedges a portfolio before an election.
Hedging always raises expected return.
Protective put
A protective put combines a long stock holding with a bought put to set a floor on loss.
A holder buys puts and limits downside.
A protective put removes the cost of insurance.
Covered call
A covered call is a long stock holding with a call sold against it, earning premium but capping upside.
A holder writes calls to earn extra income.
A covered call has unlimited upside.
Margin
Exchange-traded derivatives require margin as a deposit that covers possible losses, and it is adjusted with price moves.
A trader posts margin when buying futures.
Margin is a fee that is never refunded.
Mutual fund structure
A mutual fund is a trust that pools investor money, run by an AMC, with a trustee and a custodian providing oversight and safekeeping.
Investors hold units in a pooled trust.
A mutual fund is a company owned by its AMC.
NAV
NAV is the value of a fund's assets less liabilities divided by the units outstanding.
A fund with ₹100 crore of net assets and 10 crore units has NAV of ₹10.
NAV is set by the fund's demand in the market.
Expense ratio
The expense ratio is the annual cost of running a fund, charged as a percentage of assets and reducing returns.
A fund charges 1% a year.
Expenses are charged only when the fund makes a profit.
Derivatives in portfolios
Portfolio managers may use derivatives for hedging, portfolio rebalancing and as permitted by the agreement and regulations, with disclosure of the approach.
A manager discloses a hedging approach to clients.
Derivatives may be used freely without disclosure.

units.title: Role, registration and operations of portfolio managers
units.overview: PMS service types, SEBI registration, client onboarding, fees, custody and reporting.
facts: Portfolio manager defined
A portfolio manager is a person who, under a contract with a client, advises, directs or manages the client's securities or funds.
A registered firm manages a client's equity portfolio.
A portfolio manager manages only its own money.
Discretionary service
In a discretionary service, the manager has independent authority over the choice of investments and decisions, in the client's name, under the agreement.
The manager buys and sells without asking each time.
A discretionary manager must take client approval for each trade.
Non-discretionary service
A non-discretionary manager makes investment decisions only with the client's prior consent for each decision.
The manager calls the client before every trade.
The manager acts without client approval.
Advisory service
In an advisory service, the manager only advises on investments and the client takes the decision and executes it.
The client places the orders on the manager's advice.
The advisory manager executes trades without the client.
Registration
A portfolio manager must be registered with SEBI and must meet the eligibility, capital and fit and proper requirements.
A firm obtains a certificate before starting PMS.
Any company may offer PMS without registration.
Net worth
A portfolio manager must maintain a net worth of at least ₹5 crore, where net worth is paid-up capital and free reserves less accumulated losses and deferred expenditure not written off.
A new applicant shows capital of ₹5 crore.
The required net worth is ₹1 crore.
Minimum client investment
A client must invest at least ₹50 lakh in funds or securities with a portfolio manager, subject to exceptions such as for accredited investors.
A client opens an account with ₹60 lakh.
The minimum investment is ₹5 lakh.
Accredited investors
Accredited investors are investors recognised under the SEBI framework who may get relaxation from certain requirements, such as the minimum investment, based on their capacity.
An accredited investor invests with a lower minimum.
Every retail investor is an accredited investor.
Upfront fees
A portfolio manager may charge a fee that is fixed, return-based or a mix of both, but cannot charge an upfront fee directly or indirectly from clients.
A manager takes no fee on the day an account is opened.
Managers may collect an upfront fee when the client joins.
Segregation of client assets
Client funds and securities must be kept separate from the manager's own, with separate bank and demat accounts for clients.
Each client holds securities in an account in her name.
Client holdings may be mixed with the manager's holdings.
No guaranteed returns
A portfolio manager must not offer or imply a guaranteed return on a service.
A manager refuses to promise a return.
Managers may guarantee a minimum return.
Performance reporting
Managers must send periodic reports to clients with portfolio composition, transactions, fees and other details, at least once a quarter.
A client receives a quarterly statement.
Clients receive reports once in two years.
Disclosure document
The disclosure document gives clients the manager's investment approach, fees, risks, performance and other facts, and is filed with SEBI.
A client reads the document before signing.
A disclosure document is optional.
Principal officer
The principal officer must have the prescribed qualification, experience and a NISM certification relevant to portfolio management.
The firm names a certified principal officer.
Any employee may be principal officer without qualification.

units.title: Portfolio management process and portfolio theory
units.overview: Asset allocation, the steps of the process, and modern portfolio theory.
facts: Portfolio management process
The process includes planning with the client's objectives, executing the allocation and selection, and then feedback through monitoring and rebalancing.
A manager reviews a portfolio each quarter.
The process ends when securities are purchased.
Investment policy statement
The investment policy statement records objectives, constraints, risk profile and guidelines, and governs the manager's decisions.
A client's IPS limits equity to 60%.
An IPS is rewritten for every trade.
Strategic asset allocation
Strategic allocation sets long-term target weights across asset classes, based on objectives and risk, and is reviewed infrequently.
A target of 60% equity and 40% debt.
Strategic allocation changes with every market move.
Tactical asset allocation
Tactical allocation makes short-term deviations from strategic weights to exploit market views.
A manager holds extra cash when valuations are stretched.
Tactical allocation is the long-term target.
Correlation
Correlation measures how two returns move together, and combining assets with low correlation reduces portfolio risk.
Gold and equity often move differently.
Combining assets cannot reduce risk.
Portfolio return
The expected return of a portfolio is the weighted average of the expected returns of its assets.
50% at 10% and 50% at 6% gives 8%.
Portfolio return is the simple sum of asset returns.
Portfolio variance
Portfolio variance depends on each asset's risk, its weight and the correlation between assets, so it is not a simple average of risks.
Two risky assets with low correlation give a portfolio less risky than the average.
Portfolio risk is always the weighted average of the asset risks.
Efficient frontier
The efficient frontier shows portfolios that give the highest expected return for each level of risk.
A portfolio below the frontier gives too little return for its risk.
Every portfolio lies on the efficient frontier.
Risk-averse investor
A risk-averse investor needs more expected return to accept more risk and prefers the less risky choice for the same return.
An investor picks the safer of two equal-return options.
A risk-averse investor ignores risk.
Diversification
Diversification spreads capital across assets so that specific risk falls, but it does not remove market risk.
Holding 30 stocks lowers company-specific risk.
Diversification removes all risk.
Systematic and unsystematic risk
Systematic risk affects the whole market and cannot be diversified, while unsystematic risk is specific to a company or sector and can be.
A recession hits all stocks.
Unsystematic risk cannot be reduced by diversification.

units.title: Capital market theory and factor models
units.overview: The capital market line, CAPM, the security market line and multi-factor models.
facts: Capital market line
The CML shows the risk-return trade-off of efficient portfolios that combine the risk-free asset with the market portfolio.
An investor mixes cash with the market portfolio.
The CML applies to individual securities.
Market portfolio
The market portfolio contains all risky assets in proportion to their market value and is the tangency portfolio in the theory.
An index is used as a proxy for the market.
The market portfolio has no risk.
Beta
Beta measures a security's sensitivity to market movements, with a beta above 1 meaning more volatile than the market.
A stock with beta 1.4 rises 14% when the market rises 10%.
Beta measures total risk including specific risk.
CAPM
CAPM says expected return equals the risk-free rate plus beta times the market risk premium.
With 7% risk-free, 6% premium and beta 1.5, the expected return is 16%.
CAPM says return depends on total standard deviation.
Security market line
The SML plots expected return against beta, and securities above the line are undervalued.
A stock with a positive alpha plots above the SML.
The SML plots return against standard deviation.
Alpha
Alpha is the return earned above what CAPM predicts for the risk taken, and is a measure of manager skill.
A fund beats its CAPM return by 2%.
Alpha is the market return.
Market risk premium
The market risk premium is the expected return of the market over the risk-free rate.
If the market returns 13% and the risk-free is 7%, the premium is 6%.
The premium is the risk-free rate.
Multi-factor models
Multi-factor models explain returns with several factors, such as size, value and momentum, in addition to the market.
A model uses value and momentum in addition to beta.
Multi-factor models use only the market factor.
Capital allocation
An investor can raise return along the CML by borrowing and investing more in the market portfolio, which also raises risk.
A leveraged investor holds more than 100% in the market portfolio.
Borrowing lowers the risk of the portfolio.

units.title: Market efficiency and behavioural finance
units.overview: How efficient markets are, anomalies, and the biases that affect investors.
facts: Efficient market hypothesis
Under the efficient market hypothesis, prices reflect available information, making it hard to earn excess returns consistently.
A manager finds it hard to beat the index after costs.
Prices never reflect any information.
Weak form
Weak form efficiency says current prices reflect all past price data, so technical analysis cannot earn excess returns.
Chart patterns give no edge in a weak form market.
Weak form efficiency says insider information is already in the price.
Semi-strong form
Semi-strong efficiency says prices reflect all public information, so fundamental analysis of public data cannot earn excess returns.
Published results are priced in quickly.
Semi-strong efficiency includes private information.
Strong form
Strong form efficiency says prices reflect all information, public and private, so even insiders cannot earn excess returns.
Even insider information gives no advantage.
Strong form efficiency covers only past prices.
Random walk
A random walk means price changes are unpredictable because new information arrives randomly.
Tomorrow's price change cannot be forecast from today's.
A random walk means prices follow a fixed pattern.
Market anomalies
Anomalies, such as size and value effects, are patterns that appear to contradict market efficiency.
Small stocks have earned more than large over long periods.
Anomalies prove that markets are perfectly efficient.
Overconfidence
Overconfidence is overestimating one's own skill and information, which can lead to excess trading.
An investor trades often, sure of her views.
Overconfidence leads to under-trading.
Loss aversion
Loss aversion is the tendency to feel losses more strongly than equal gains, which can lead to holding losers.
An investor refuses to sell a falling stock.
Loss aversion makes investors sell losers quickly.
Herding
Herding is following the crowd rather than one's own analysis, which can feed bubbles.
Investors rush into a hot sector.
Herding is independent analysis.
Anchoring
Anchoring is holding on to an initial reference, such as a purchase price, when making later decisions.
An investor waits for the price to return to her cost.
Anchoring updates views fully on new data.

units.title: Risk and risk management
units.overview: Types of risk, measurement tools and how managers control risk.
facts: Risk management process
Risk management is identifying, measuring, monitoring and controlling risks relative to the portfolio's objectives.
A manager sets limits and checks them daily.
Risk management means avoiding all risk.
Standard deviation
Standard deviation measures how widely returns vary around their average and is the common measure of total risk.
A higher standard deviation means a more volatile fund.
Standard deviation measures only downside.
Value at Risk
VaR estimates the largest loss expected over a period at a stated confidence level, under normal conditions.
A one-day 95% VaR of ₹2 lakh.
VaR is the maximum possible loss.
Maximum drawdown
Maximum drawdown is the largest peak-to-trough fall in value over a period, showing the worst loss experienced.
A fund falls from ₹120 to ₹90 before recovering.
Drawdown is the average annual loss.
Tracking error
Tracking error is the standard deviation of the difference between portfolio and benchmark returns, measuring active risk.
A fund with a tracking error of 3% deviates from its index.
Tracking error measures market risk.
Liquidity risk
Liquidity risk is the risk of being unable to sell a position quickly without a large price concession.
A manager cannot exit a small-cap holding without moving the price.
Liquidity risk applies only to bonds.
Concentration risk
Concentration risk arises when a large part of the portfolio is in a few securities or sectors.
A portfolio holds 40% in one sector.
Concentration reduces risk.
Counterparty risk
Counterparty risk is the risk that the other party to a contract fails to meet its obligation.
A derivative contract is traded over the counter.
Exchange-traded trades carry no counterparty protection.
Stress testing
Stress testing evaluates portfolio losses under extreme but plausible scenarios, complementing statistical measures.
A manager tests a 30% market fall.
Stress tests use only normal markets.
Operational risk
Operational risk is the risk of loss from failed processes, people, systems or external events, including errors and fraud.
A trade is mistakenly entered twice.
Operational risk arises only from market moves.
Risk limits
Risk limits, such as caps on single-stock and sector exposure, keep the portfolio within the client's agreed risk profile.
A manager limits a stock to 10%.
Limits are set after losses occur.

units.title: Equity and fixed income portfolio strategies
units.overview: Passive and active approaches, smart beta, core-satellite, and bond portfolio strategies.
facts: Passive strategy
A passive strategy replicates an index to match its return at low cost without trying to outperform.
A portfolio holds the index stocks in index weights.
A passive strategy seeks to beat the index.
Active strategy
An active strategy departs from the benchmark to earn higher returns, at higher cost and risk of underperformance.
A manager overweights chosen stocks.
Active strategies guarantee outperformance.
Smart beta
Smart beta uses rules-based weights based on factors such as value or low volatility instead of market capitalisation.
An index weights stocks by earnings rather than size.
Smart beta is a market-cap weighted index.
Factor investing
Factor investing targets return drivers such as value, momentum, quality and size across stocks.
A portfolio tilts to high-quality stocks.
Factor investing ignores stock characteristics.
Core-satellite
A core-satellite approach holds a low-cost core, often passive, with smaller active satellites to seek extra return.
A manager holds an index core and a few active bets.
Core-satellite is 100% active.
Growth and value styles
Growth investing seeks firms with high earnings growth, while value investing seeks stocks trading below their estimated worth.
A manager buys a low P/E stock with solid earnings.
Value investing seeks the highest P/E.
Bond immunisation
Immunisation matches the portfolio's duration to the liability horizon so that interest rate changes have little net effect.
A manager matches duration to a payout date.
Immunisation aims to maximise rate bets.
Laddering
A bond ladder spreads holdings evenly across maturities to manage reinvestment and interest rate risk.
Bonds mature every year.
A ladder puts all funds in one maturity.
Barbell and bullet
A barbell holds short and long maturities, while a bullet concentrates holdings around one maturity.
A barbell skips the intermediate bonds.
A bullet spreads across all maturities.
Active bond management
Active bond managers use views on rates, curve shape and credit spreads to earn more than the benchmark.
A manager lengthens duration before rates fall.
Active bond managers never change duration.
Derivative overlay
Derivatives can be overlaid on a portfolio to adjust exposure or protect it without selling the underlying securities.
A manager sells index futures to cut equity exposure.
Overlays require selling all holdings.

units.title: Performance measurement, attribution and valuation
units.overview: Return calculation, risk-adjusted measures, attribution, benchmarking, GIPS and valuing securities.
facts: Time-weighted return
TWRR removes the effect of the timing and size of client cash flows, so it measures the manager's skill.
A manager is measured regardless of client deposits.
TWRR depends on when the client adds money.
Money-weighted return
The money-weighted return is the internal rate of return and is affected by the timing of cash flows.
A client's return is lower after a late deposit before a fall.
MWRR is independent of cash flow timing.
Sharpe ratio
The Sharpe ratio is excess return over the risk-free rate divided by standard deviation, showing return per unit of total risk.
A fund returns 12% with 7% risk-free and 10% deviation, giving 0.5.
The Sharpe ratio uses beta as risk.
Treynor ratio
The Treynor ratio is excess return over the risk-free rate divided by beta, showing return per unit of systematic risk.
A fund earns 5% excess with beta 1.25, giving 4%.
The Treynor ratio uses total risk.
Jensen's alpha
Jensen's alpha is the portfolio return less the CAPM expected return, and a positive value means outperformance for the beta taken.
A fund earns 3% above its CAPM return.
A negative alpha shows outperformance.
Information ratio
The information ratio is active return divided by tracking error, showing return per unit of active risk.
A manager earns 2% active return with 4% tracking error, giving 0.5.
The information ratio uses market risk.
Benchmark selection
A good benchmark is appropriate, investable, measurable and specified in advance, and reflects the manager's style.
A large-cap manager uses a large-cap index.
Any index can serve as a benchmark.
Performance attribution
Attribution splits excess return into sources such as asset allocation, security selection and interaction.
A report shows that stock selection added most of the outperformance.
Attribution shows only total return.
GIPS
GIPS are voluntary global standards for fair presentation and full disclosure of investment performance.
A firm presents performance in line with GIPS.
GIPS are laws enforced by SEBI.
Valuation of securities
Securities in a portfolio are valued as per the norms in the regulations and the agreement, using market prices, and fair value where none exist.
A listed share is valued at its closing price.
Each manager may value securities as it likes.
Standardised PMS performance
SEBI requires portfolio manager performance to be reported on a uniform basis, with returns computed using TWRR through a central platform.
Managers' reported returns are comparable.
Each manager chooses its own method freely.

units.title: Rebalancing, taxation, regulation and ethics
units.overview: Why and how portfolios are rebalanced, tax in the client's hands, and the conduct and legal obligations of managers.
facts: Need for rebalancing
Rebalancing restores target weights when market moves cause drift, keeping risk in line with the policy.
Equity rises to 70% against a 60% target and is trimmed.
Rebalancing is needed only if returns are negative.
Calendar and threshold rebalancing
Calendar rebalancing occurs at set times, while threshold rebalancing occurs when weights drift beyond set limits.
A manager rebalances when weight exceeds a 5% band.
Both methods use the same trigger.
Costs of rebalancing
Rebalancing creates transaction costs and may create tax, which must be weighed against the benefit of risk control.
A small drift is left to avoid costs.
Rebalancing has no cost.
Constant mix and buy-and-hold
A constant mix strategy keeps fixed weights by selling winners and buying losers, while buy-and-hold lets weights drift.
A manager sells equity after a rally to restore 60%.
Buy-and-hold keeps weights fixed.
CPPI
Constant proportion portfolio insurance moves money between a risky and a safe asset based on a floor, raising risk as the cushion grows.
A manager sells equity as value nears the floor.
CPPI buys more risk as the cushion shrinks.
Taxation in client's hands
Because PMS holdings are in the client's name, gains, dividends and losses are taxed in the client's hands.
A client reports gains from sales by the manager.
The manager pays tax on behalf of all clients.
Section 9A
Section 9A provides that an eligible offshore fund is not treated as having a business connection in India just because its fund manager operates here, if conditions are met.
A fund manager in India manages an offshore fund.
Section 9A applies to every domestic client.
Insider trading
Trading on unpublished price-sensitive information is prohibited, and managers must have policies to prevent misuse.
A manager does not trade on confidential results.
Insider trading rules do not apply to managers.
Front running
Front running is trading ahead of a client's large order for the manager's own benefit and is a prohibited practice.
A dealer buys before a client's block order.
Front running is acceptable if disclosed in a note.
Anti-money laundering
Managers must follow know-your-client and anti-money laundering norms, verify identity and report suspicious transactions.
A firm collects KYC before onboarding.
AML norms apply only to banks.
Fiduciary duty and conflicts
The manager must act in clients' best interest, disclose conflicts and treat clients fairly in allocating trades.
A manager allocates a trade fairly across accounts.
A manager may favour its own proprietary account.
Investor charter and grievances
Clients have rights under the investor charter and can seek redress from the manager, then SEBI's complaint platform and online dispute resolution.
An unhappy client escalates to the regulator's portal.
Clients have no recourse beyond the manager.
